[THOUGHT] The patient has a several-month history of discrete red-brown papules with fine mica-like scale on the ventral arms and legs that resolve leaving post-inflammatory hypopigmentation. The chronicity (≈4 months), small scaly erythematous-to-brown papules, proximal-extremity distribution, and residual lighter macules strongly favor a chronic papulosquamous inflammatory dermatosis. Wood's lamp is normal (argues against tinea versicolor/vitiligo), there is no clear mucosal involvement or classic violaceous, polygonal lesions to suggest lichen planus, and the morphology and course are typical for pityriasis lichenoides chronica (the chronic variant of pityriasis lichenoides), which commonly produces persistent small scaly papules and post-inflammatory hypo- or hyperpigmentation. A biopsy was performed (appropriate) but even without histology the clinical picture is most consistent with pityriasis lichenoides chronica.

[DIAGNOSIS] Pityriasis lichenoides chronica (chronic pityriasis lichenoides)

[THOUGHT] The clinical presentation (months-long course, recurrent red‑brown papules with a mica‑like scale on the limbs, post‑inflammatory hypopigmentation) is compatible with pityriasis lichenoides chronica (PLC). However, several critical differential diagnoses — especially mycosis fungoides (pityriasis lichenoides–like MF), parapsoriasis, secondary syphilis, and tinea—can present similarly and require specific testing to exclude. A punch biopsy was done but histopathology results are not provided; histology (and, when indicated, immunophenotyping/T‑cell clonality) is essential to distinguish PLC from MF and other mimics. Other missing/critical items: fungal testing (KOH/culture), syphilis serology if risk factors present, and a focused mucosal/genital exam and sexual history. These missing data are red flags because misdiagnosis could delay treatment for potentially more serious conditions (esp. MF or syphilis).

- Red flag / critical missing tests: punch biopsy histopathology (H&E) and, if atypia suspected, immunohistochemistry and T‑cell receptor clonality; KOH/fungal testing; syphilis serology; clear mucosal/genital exam and sexual history; documentation of pruritus/scale history and response to any prior therapies.

4. Focused mucosal/genital examination and sexual history (document presence/absence of mucosal lesions).
5. Clarify symptom details: presence/degree of pruritus, any temporal pattern, prior treatments and responses.
6. Provide the clinical photographs and, if biopsy is nondiagnostic, consider repeat/deeper biopsy.

After these data are available, reassess — if histology is consistent with PLC and other testing is negative, then PASS would be appropriate.
